x: ← Project Scroll About About Project Scroll Project Scroll is independent historical research: an online treasure hunt anyone can play, a research desk anyone can hire, and a studio for digital imaging, design, photography, 3D LiDAR, animation and video. All of it runs on one rule. Every clue is true, and every answer is in the record. Who we are Project Scroll is run by an independent researcher and author who writes narrative nonfiction about the history of the Great Lakes country, and who trained in visual communications. The research behind that writing is the same research we offer you: old certificates, deeds, surveys, county histories and newspapers, read line by line and compared until they agree, or until we can say exactly why they don’t. What we offer Professional research. Lost ancestors, family histories and registers, family legends tested against the record, forgotten places, maps and land surveys, heirlooms, lodges and old societies, historical research for authors, films and local groups, and a second pair of eyes on anything you mean to publish. Research services . Imaging, design and video. Digital imaging of photographs, documents, maps and heirlooms; imaging analysis of faded ink, damaged pages and the details in old photographs; image creation and restoration; graphic design for family books, charts, covers and keepsakes; photography; and video production, from family-history films to recorded interviews. 3D and living documents. Landscapes modeled in three dimensions from public LiDAR elevation surveys, 3D animations and fly-throughs, every reconstruction labeled as one, and living documents: research papers, timelines and family records that keep growing as new evidence turns up, with every change dated. The studio . Every commission starts with an honest first read: what can be done, and what it will take, before you commit to anything. What we believe The record decides. Not the family tree online, not the story everybody tells, not what we hoped to find. Every statement is marked. You can always see whether a fact comes from a document, a book, a family story or our own reading. How we mark the evidence . Gaps are shown, not filled. An honest “not yet known” is worth more than a confident guess. Corrections are welcome. If you know better, tell us. The record is bigger than any one of us. Places and people are respected. The hunt never asks anyone to dig, to disturb a grave or a mound, or to go looking for anyone’s home. When we get something wrong We will. When a reader or a new document shows that a page of this site is mistaken, we change the page, date the change on it, and say what was wrong, rather than quietly replacing the words. A case that was called solved on a bad reading is reopened and says so. If you have found an error, write to research@projectscroll.com or tell us on Facebook; corrections are credited to the person who sent them, by name or not, as they prefer. The record behind this site The dates on the scroll, the person of the month and the then-and-now maps are built from the same sources the hunt asks you to open: Rogers (1875), Mathews (1882), Glover (1906), the 1860 wall map at the Library of Congress, and Michigan death certificates at the Archives of Michigan. Where a page of this site makes a claim, the source is on the page or one click away. If it is not, that is a correction we owe. Where it started Project Scroll began in Cassopolis, Michigan , with a few questions the county history couldn’t answer. It doesn’t stop there. The hunt and the desk now take on questions from anywhere the records reach. Play the hunt Research services Imaging, design and video Get in touch

← Project Scroll For every reader Accessibility The hunt is open to anyone, anywhere, and that includes anyone who reads with a keyboard, a screen reader, a magnifier, captions or a steady page. We aim to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA, and we test every change against them. What is built in Keyboard. Every link, button, filter, map control and dialog works from the keyboard. A “Skip to the content” link is the first thing on every page. Press / or Ctrl K to search. Screen readers. Pages use real headings, landmarks and labels. Pictures carry text descriptions; decorative ornaments are hidden from screen readers. Motion. If your device asks for reduced motion, the gold leaf, glints, rolling place names and drawn trails hold still. The Pause all motion switch at the foot of every page does the same on any device, and remembers your choice. Light and dark. The site follows your device, and the moon button switches by hand. Text and controls are checked for contrast in both. Listening. The Listen buttons read a section aloud with your device’s own voice. Text size. Zoom to 200% or more and the page reflows to one column without sideways scrolling. Print. Every page prints cleanly, without the animations and controls. What is harder, and how we help The deep-zoom maps in the map room are pictures served by the Library of Congress. Their town names and directories are given in text beside them, and we will read any part of a map for you on request. Old handwriting and print. Certificates and book pages are shown as pictures. Where a page is the subject of a case, its key lines are transcribed in the text; ask, and we will transcribe any page you need. Facebook. Clues are posted on Facebook, whose accessibility is Meta’s. Every case also has its own page here. Tell us If anything on Project Scroll is hard to use, write to research@projectscroll.com with the page and what happened. We answer, and we fix what we can. Last reviewed 20 October 2026.

← Project Scroll Cass County, Michigan Cassopolis, Michigan: its history, in the record Cassopolis is the county seat of Cass County, Michigan, platted in 1831 and named for Lewis Cass, then governor of Michigan Territory. This page gathers what Project Scroll has opened so far on the village and its county: the maps, the county histories, the certificates and the newspapers, with a link to each record where it is held. The village at a glance Founded: platted 1831; chosen as county seat the same year, a compromise between rival settlements. Named for: Lewis Cass (1782–1866), governor of Michigan Territory 1813–31, later Secretary of War and of State. First published histories: Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (Cassopolis, 1875); Alfred Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (Chicago, 1882); L. H. Glover, A Twentieth Century History of Cass County (Chicago, 1906). On the map: the 1860 Geil & Harley wall map of Cass County, held by the Library of Congress, carries a plan of the village with lot numbers and owners; you can lay it over today’s streets , and the county’s township sheets of about 1928 are in the map room . Vital records: Michigan death certificates from 1897 are free to read at the Archives of Michigan; here is how to read one . Who kept the village in 1860: two hotels, three merchants and three physicians, engraved beside the Cassopolis plan on the county wall map. Geil, Harley & Siverd, 1860 · Library of Congress What the hunt has found in Cassopolis The hunt began here, with a joke secret society of 1846 whose story is told in Rogers and Mathews, a village hotel that was hauled across town and turned into a mill, and a doctor who kept a bone. Each is an open case on the case board ; the first two are listed here, and each has its sources free online. Did the joke lodge of 1846 ever have a real charter? Where did the Union Hotel go when it became a mill? Document of the month: one page of Rogers, 1875, read slowly A field note: one letter, two certificates Next door, 1860 and 1928 Penn Township is the ground just east of the village, with Diamond Lake in its south-west corner and Vandalia on the railroad. Here it is twice: as the 1860 wall map engraved it, and as a plat book drew it about 1928. The square mile sections are the same, so the two line up. Slide across and watch sixty-eight years of owners change hands. 1860 c. 1928 Penn Township, 1860 and about 1928. Geil, Harley & Siverd, 1860, Library of Congress · plat book, about 1928, Cass County MIGenWeb A challenge Find the families who stayed Ten surnames are written on this township in both years: on a farm in 1860, and still on the land about 1928. Find them. Slide the map, read the names, and type each one you find. A surname on both maps The hotel corner, thirty years on In 1860 the engraver wrote one word on the block by the court house: HOTEL. Twenty-four years later the Sanborn Map Company drew the same corner building by building, for the insurers. ← Project Scroll From the desk The glossary The words old records use, and the words we use about them, in plain English. Learn a handful, and an old deed or gravestone starts to talk. Find a word Abstract A summary of a document, such as a deed or will, giving its main points. Useful for finding the original, but not the record itself: abstracts drop words and sometimes get names and dates wrong. Administrator The person a court appoints to settle the estate of someone who died without a will. Compare executor. Ahnentafel German for “ancestor table.” A numbering system for a pedigree: the subject is 1, a person’s father is double their number and their mother double plus one. So 2 is the father, 3 the mother, 4 the father’s father. Census A count of the population. The United States has taken one every ten years since 1790; from 1850 it names every free person in the household (enslaved people were counted on separate schedules, usually without names, until 1870). Most of the 1890 census was destroyed after a fire in 1921. Each census is opened to the public 72 years after it was taken. Consort A husband or wife. Often seen on old gravestones: “Mary, consort of John Smith.” County history The big county histories printed from the 1870s to the 1910s. Many biographies in them were paid for by the people they describe, so they tend to be reliable on what the family knew well, and generous on everything else; dates and places still need a document. Deed The written record of land changing hands, copied into the county’s deed books. Deeds often name wives, heirs and neighbors, and sometimes say where a seller had moved to. Ditto (do.) “The same as above.” Census takers and clerks used it, or a pair of marks, for repeated surnames, birthplaces and occupations. Double dating Dates such as “10 February 1731/2.” Before 1752, England and its colonies began the new year on 25 March, so January to March dates were often written with both years. Et ux. Latin, “and wife,” in deeds and court records: “John Smith et ux.” means John and his wife. Executor The person named in a will to carry it out. Compare administrator. Field notes A surveyor’s notebook from the original land survey, recording every line walked: the trees, streams, soil and sometimes the people met along the way. General Land Office The federal office that surveyed and sold public land, from 1812 until it became part of the Bureau of Land Management in 1946. Its plats, field notes and patents are free online. Informant The person who answered the questions on a certificate. On a death certificate the dead person was never the informant, so everything on it is someone else’s memory. Instant and ultimo Old newspaper shorthand: “the 4th inst.” means the 4th of this month; “the 20th ult.” the 20th of last month. Intestate Having died without a will. The court then appoints an administrator and divides the estate by law. Land patent The first transfer of a piece of land from the government to a private owner. Local legend The famous ancestor, the buried treasure, the river under the ground. Some are true. The desk reads each one against the record and says which. Long s (ſ) An s that looks like an f without the full crossbar, used at the start or in the middle of a word until about 1800. “Congreſs” is Congress. Lore What a place says about itself: the stories passed around a lake, a township or a lodge, told without a page to point to. Lore is where a hunt often starts; the record is where it ends. Maiden name A woman’s surname before marriage. Most records name married women only by their husbands’ surnames, which is why a woman’s own family is the commonest gap in any tree. mtDNA and Y-DNA Two DNA tests that follow one line each: mitochondrial DNA passes from mother to child down the all-female line; Y-DNA passes from father to son down the all-male line. x: ← The hunter’s toolkit A guide from the desk How do I read old handwriting in records? The writing in old records is not hard once you know ten tricks the clerks used. Here they are, with a short quiz at the end. The clerks’ tricks ſ The long s Looks like an f without the full crossbar. Used at the start or middle of a word until about 1800: “Congreſs”, “ſon”, “Miſsiſsippi”. Read it as an ordinary s. ye “Ye” means “the” The y stands for an old letter, thorn (þ), pronounced “th”. “Ye olde inn” was always read “the old inn”. Likewise “yt” = that, “ym” = them. Wm · Jno · Chas Shortened first names Clerks raised the last letters: Wm = William, Jno = John (not Jonathan), Chas = Charles, Thos = Thomas, Jas = James, Geo = George, Saml = Samuel, Benj = Benjamin. inst. · ult. · prox. Which month? “The 4th inst.” = the 4th of this month. “The 20th ult.” = the 20th of last month. “The 2nd prox.” = the 2nd of next month. Check the date of the letter or newspaper to know which month. do. Ditto “do.” under an entry means “the same as above.” Census takers and clerks used it for repeated surnames, birthplaces and occupations. &c. Et cetera The ampersand plus c: “and so on”. Often written as a looped sign that can look like a letter. 1745/6 Double dates Before 1752 in England and its colonies, the new year began on 25 March. A date between January and March is often written with both years. Use the later one for today’s calendar. relict · consort On gravestones “Relict of John Smith” = his widow (she outlived him). “Consort of” = his wife, who died while he was living. dec’d · Esq. In deeds and wills dec’d = deceased. Esq. = Esquire, a courtesy for a lawyer or a man of standing, not a title of nobility. 71y 4m 12d Ages to the day Age at death in years, months and days. Count back from the date of death with the age calculator . Test yourself Six questions. A letter dated 10 June says “your note of the 28th ult.” When was the note written? “ult.” means last month: 28 May. In a 1790 newspaper you read “Congreſs”. What does it say? That f-like letter is the long s. A census line reads “Jno Smith” and below it “do. do.” What is the second person’s name? Jno is John, and do. repeats the line above. A gravestone reads “Mary, relict of Amos Hale.” What does it tell you? A relict outlived her husband. A baptism is dated “12 February 1734/5”. Which year is it on today’s calendar? Part VI How we mark the evidence Not every source is worth the same. A death certificate filed the week a man died is not a story his grandson told sixty years later, and neither of them is our own opinion. So in every research report, every statement carries one of nine marks, strongest first. You can see at a glance what the record says, and what we are arguing from it. Strongest Weakest What the record says What we argue from it What the record says Document Made at the time, by someone whose job was to write it down: a death certificate, a deed, a census page, a survey, a map. Example: a 1912 Michigan death certificate. Period print Printed at or near the time: a newspaper notice, an obituary, a book of the day. Example: a doctor’s obituary printed the year he died. County history The big county histories of the 1870s to the 1910s. Rich and indispensable, but often written decades later from what families remembered, and rarely checked. Example: the 1882 History of Cass County. Compiled A later hand gathering earlier records: an index, a bibliography, a transcription, a modern summary. Good for finding things; we go back to the original whenever it survives. Example: a trail-diary bibliography that lists an unpublished typescript. Tradition What a family or a community says, passed down by word of mouth. Worth recording exactly as told, and worth testing. Example: “Grandpa always said he came over on the last boat before the war.” Field What we saw or measured ourselves, at first hand, dated, from public ground or with permission. Example: a dated photograph of a marker on a public roadside. What we argue from it Inference A step that follows directly from the records. Example: one certificate was filed a month after he died, the other twenty-three years later, so the first informant was closer to the event. Reading Our interpretation of what the records point to. Always labeled, always open to correction. Example: “In 1935, someone gave the father his son’s initial.” Hypothesis An idea worth testing that the records don’t yet support. We say what would prove or disprove it. Example: he never used a middle initial at all; his obituary and gravestone would tell. Marks, strongest first: Document Period print County history Compiled Tradition Field (seen at first hand) Inference Reading Hypothesis — the last three marks are our own argument, offered for correction How it looks in a report A pioneer died in Michigan in 1912. His death certificate gives no middle initial Document . A county history adds “Senior” to his name County history . His son’s death certificate, filled in twenty-three years later, gives the father a middle initial: the son’s own Document . The first informant was closer to the event Inference . Father and son shared a name, and in 1935 someone gave the father the son’s initial too Reading . Or he never used a middle initial at all, which his obituary would show Hypothesis . Tap a mark to see what it means. From our case “ One Letter, Two Certificates .” Every report you receive from us is marked the same way. Weigh the evidence Add records to each side and watch the scale. Records are weighed, not counted: one good document can outweigh a pile of family stories. Side A Side B The scale is level. Add a record to either side. The weights are a rule of thumb, not a formula: a late or careless document can still be wrong, and a detailed tradition can still be right. ← Research services Mysteries in the family Is the family story true? Every family has a story that has been told so often nobody questions it. Some are true. Some are half-true. Some began as a guess a hundred years ago. The records can usually tell which. Test a family legend Choose the story your family tells. Pick a story above to see what the records usually say about it, and how we would test yours. Tradition What families say. An inspector couldn’t spell it, so he wrote down something easier, and that became the family name. Document What the records usually show. Ellis Island inspectors did not write names down; they checked arrivals against passenger lists made at the port of departure. Names did change, often, but usually years later and by the family itself: at naturalization, at work, at school, or simply over time. How we test it Find the passenger list: it shows the name as written where the journey began. Find the naturalization papers, which often record both the old name and the new one. Follow the name census by census to see when the new spelling first appears. Reading The change almost always happened. Ellis Island almost never did it. Tradition What families say. A lord, a king, a governor or a famous founder sits at the top of the tree. Document What the records usually show. Some of these are true. Many began as a name match: someone of the right surname, in roughly the right place, adopted into the tree a century ago and copied forward until it looked like fact. How we test it Test the line one link at a time, starting with the most recent. Every parent–child joint needs its own record. Find who first printed the claim, and what they cited. Check the famous person’s documented children against the one the family claims. Reading Worth testing. Usually the line breaks at one particular joint, and finding it is a story in itself. Tradition What families say. A grandmother or great-grandmother was a Native princess, often said to be Cherokee. Document What the records usually show. The Cherokee Nation did not have princesses, and the story is so widespread that historians treat it as a family-legend pattern of its own. Some families do have Native ancestry, and the records that show it are specific: tribal rolls, agency censuses and treaty and allotment papers. How we test it Name the ancestor and place her in a census, with the people around her. Search the tribal rolls of the place and period (for the Cherokee: the Dawes and Guion Miller rolls, and the earlier rolls before them). A DNA test cannot show tribal membership; only the records and the nation itself can. Reading The princess is almost never real. The ancestor sometimes is, and deserves to be found properly. Tradition What families say. Three brothers arrived on one ship: one went north, one went south and one went west. Document What the records usually show. It is one of the most common stories in American family lore. Sometimes there were three brothers. Often there were three men of the same surname who were not related at all, later joined together to explain why the name turns up in different places. How we test it Find each man separately in the passenger lists, censuses and land records. Look for a document that names them as brothers: a will, a deed, a probate file. For male lines, a Y-DNA test can say whether their descendants share a father at all. Reading Often half-true: the men were real; the brotherhood is the part to test. Tradition What families say. Everything was lost in the fire, so there is no point looking. Document What the records usually show. Courthouses did burn, and records were lost. But deeds were often re-recorded afterward by the owners, and copies survive in state archives, churches, newspapers, tax rolls, military files and the records of neighboring counties. The case A pioneer died in Michigan in 1912. The old county histories give him a plain first and last name. One of them adds “Senior.” County history His own death certificate, filed about a month after he died, gives the same plain name. No initial at all. Document Then we found his son’s death certificate, from 1935. In the box for the father’s name, whoever answered the questions gave him a middle initial: the same one the son carried. Document So which is right? Make your guess now. Ours is further down. Then it got stranger Once we started comparing every box, the records kept arguing. His birthday: his death certificate and one of the county histories are two days apart. His father’s birthplace: the certificate names one state. That same history names another. One man, one family and three disagreements. Nobody lied. Each one is somebody’s memory. What this teaches Every record was written by someone. A death certificate tells you what the informant believed, on a hard day. Their name is usually on it. The father’s was filed about a month after he died; the son’s was filled in twenty-three years later, by someone remembering a man long gone. County histories have the same weakness: the family usually supplied the facts, often from memory, and nobody checked them. One letter can change everything. Fathers and sons with the same name get tangled in the record all the time. One wrong initial can merge two men or split one, and send you chasing somebody else’s family for a month. Watch out for “Senior.” In the 1800s it didn’t always mean “father.” Sometimes it only meant the older of two men with the same name in town, related or not. Here a son with the same name does turn up, so the label fits, but always check. Disagreement is a clue, not a failure. Every mismatch tells you who was remembering, and when. Our guess, as promised: father and son shared a name, and in 1935 someone gave the father the son’s initial too Reading . But a guess is not proof. Four rules for when records disagree Ask who gave the information, and when. Closer to the event usually weighs more, but not always. Keep looking. A third, independent record can tip the balance, but records are weighed, not counted. Write down both versions and where each came from. Never quietly “fix” one. Call it settled only when the evidence settles it. Until then, it’s an open question. Where the case stands Open Our next witness: a local newspaper notice from the days or weeks after his death. Then his probate file, and the cemetery’s burial records or a transcription of his stone. Read the stone on paper. Don’t go to it. x: ← The places Van Buren County, Michigan Paw Paw, Michigan: its history, in the record Paw Paw, the seat of Van Buren County, takes its name from the Paw Paw River and the pawpaw trees that grew along it. Rodney Hinckley took up a farm on the river in 1832, a sawmill followed in 1833, and the village was incorporated in 1837; the Van Buren County Courthouse on Paw Paw Street is on the National Register of Historic Places. The town at a glance Founded: settled 1832–33; incorporated 1837; the county seat. Name: from the Paw Paw River, itself named for the pawpaw tree. In the record: Ellis’s history of Berrien and Van Buren counties (1880) and Rowland’s of Van Buren (1912); the Paw Paw True Northerner, from the 1850s. On the map: the 1860 Geil & Harley county map carries a plan of Paw Paw; lay it over today’s streets . Wine country: grapes are the district’s crop; St. Julian and Warner Vineyards both began in Paw Paw, and the village holds a Wine and Harvest Festival each autumn. Where to look The county seat’s records — probate, deeds and the True Northerner — are the first stop for Van Buren families; the 1912 Rowland history is the fullest for the townships.
